item.title: Trump says Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets
item.description: His administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, Timothy Gardner, Jarrett Renshaw
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump said on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. Prices for diesel, used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking, are near a record and risk for Trump's fellow Republicans ahead of the November 3 congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain thin control of Congress. Diesel prices fell after the announcement, but analysts said the deal may not be enough to keep them down. Trump said on social media he had a "highly successful" discussion with President Vladimir Putin in which they agreed that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. After the call, an envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, praised cooperation between Russia and the US in a post on X. Dmitriev asked US officials during his visit to Washington last month for licenses to export diesel to the US market to be granted to all Russian major oil firms, sources familiar with the situation said. In October 2025, the US imposed sanctions on Russian oil companies over Moscow's war that began in 2022. The diesel exports could provide Moscow with billions of dollars in revenues that could help Putin continue the war with Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticized the deal, announced while a Ukrainian delegation was in the US to discuss how to seek a resolution of the war, as a "weak decision on the part of strong partners." "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," he said on X. The deal was also criticized by US lawmakers including Trump's fellow Republican, Representative Don Bacon, who said it is time to apply more sanctions that [USN:L1N4431OK TEXT:"Congress passed recently"], not lift the measures. "Now is the time to use those sanctions to squeeze Putin’s war machine, not reward a dictator by putting more money in his hands while he continues targeting and killing Ukrainian civilians," Bacon said on X. The US Treasury Department issued a license allowing importation of Russian diesel until April 7. Trump said Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Even more would follow, Trump said, "based on the condition of their diesel refineries," which have been damaged by Ukrainian attacks. 'NOTHING BURGER' Analysts said the agreement was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices. "I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is," Rory Johnston, an oil market researcher and founder of CommodityContext.com, said on X, adding that Russia usually exports much more diesel than volumes in the deal when its refinery fleet is not under attack. "It's clearly not a fix, but another stream to aid a very tight diesel market," said Jim Mitchell, an analyst at consultancy Wood Mackenzie. [USN:L1N45U0FQ TEXT:"Diesel prices"], which are often a big driver of inflation, are up 70% since the US and Israel launched the war with Iran on February 28. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered a severe global fuel supply crunch, pushing average US diesel prices to $6.28 a gallon on Thursday, according to the AAA motorist group. Prices have stayed high despite two recent moves by Trump to boost supplies of the fuel: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is normally used for farm equipment. US diesel futures fell almost 5% following news of the deal and were trading at $4.64 a gallon. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump said. DEFENSE PRODUCTION ACT Three industry sources said earlier on Friday that Trump will issue a directive in the coming days to some US department heads to find ways to control diesel prices. The directive, which they said could take the form of a presidential memo, will push officials to find ways to bypass local and state regulations blocking energy production and use the Cold War-era Defense Production Act to increase output of oil and fuel. Under the DPA, the president can authorize US-backed loans or loan guarantees to expand domestic manufacturing of critical materials and to require companies to prioritize government contracts for essential goods. The White House has been weighing how to use the DPA to expand refining capacity as the war with Iran exposes US vulnerability to supply disruptions and price spikes. Refining executives [USN:L1N45214P TEXT:"told administration officials"] last month that federal money would be better directed toward making refineries more efficient or expanding plants rather than financing a new refinery, which would be more costly and take years to complete.

item.title: Tesla renames 'Full Self-Driving' to 'Assisted Driving' in Europe as it chases clearance for software
item.description: Several regulators have said the old name is misleading.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: EV-maker Tesla (TSLA.O) has started calling its "Full Self-Driving" feature "Tesla Assisted Driving" on its European websites, dropping a name regulators have said was [USN:L6N41E09R TEXT:"misleading"], as CEO Elon Musk pushes for EU-wide approval for the software. The rebrand comes after Germany said on Tuesday Tesla had [USN:L6N45T0YE TEXT:"offered to switch to the new name"]. Musk has described the self-driving technology as key to the company's future growth. Tesla's FSD page for Slovakia now redirects to a "Tesla Assisted Driving" page, as do pages in other European countries such as Germany, Spain and the Netherlands. The US site still refers to it as "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)." A Reuters [USN:L6N45R0YL TEXT:"report"] published this week detailed how Tesla mounted a campaign to win approval for FSD in Europe, including encouraging owners and supporters to lobby national regulators for faster approvals. In September, a Norwegian Tesla owner asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration whether Tesla's changes to how it described FSD addressed concerns about the name, according to documents Reuters obtained through freedom-of-information requests. "Please do not simply say again that 'we are waiting for the EU' without explaining what Tesla or Norway must deliver in the meantime," the owner said. Several regulators have said the old name is misleading because the system requires constant supervision and drivers remain legally responsible. In Sweden, consumer protection authorities had earlier asked the Swedish Transport Agency to assess whether the marketing of FSD could give buyers the false impression the system was capable of fully autonomous driving. In Italy, authorities had said in internal government correspondence that the name "Full Self-Driving", together with Tesla's promotional material, "could lead users to believe that the vehicle is equipped with unsupervised automatic driving functions attributable to higher levels of automation, particularly SAE Level 3", in communication seen by Reuters through freedom-of-information requests. Eight EU countries already allow the system, with [USN:L8N45U0I2 TEXT:"Slovakia"] expecting to become the ninth within days. An EU-wide vote has been [USN:L6N45H0TX TEXT:"pushed"] from October to at least December, with countries like France conducting [USN:L6N44V0W3 TEXT:"additional"] testing.

item.title: How the US plan to livestream an execution compares with global practice
item.description: If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution. Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage. HAS A LAWFUL EXECUTION EVER BEEN LIVESTREAMED OR BROADCAST TO THE PUBLIC BEFORE? Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience. Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live. Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions. HOW UNUSUAL IS THIS COMPARED WITH MODERN EXECUTION PRACTICES AROUND THE WORLD? Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view. According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan. The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936. Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during World War Two. HOW HAS THE INTERNET CHANGED THE CIRCULATION OF EXECUTION FOOTAGE? The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes. Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools. Criminal organisations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power. The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material. WHAT HAS BEEN THE REACTION FROM GOVERNMENTS AND TECH COMPANIES? Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage. Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organisations and other violent groups. One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place. Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene. Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019. (This story has been corrected to fix the year to 2001, not 2021, in paragraph 15.)

item.title: US immigration chiefs defend shooting of New York man, attack 'sanctuary' policies
item.description: US immigration officials defended federal agents on Friday who shot and wounded a New York City man in his car with a young child believed to be his son in the back seat and rebuked Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his condemnation of immigration agents.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Allen, Joseph Ax
item.content:encoded: US immigration officials defended federal agents on Friday who shot and wounded a New York City man in his car with a young child believed to be his son in the back seat and rebuked Mayor Zohran Mamdani for his condemnation of immigration agents. US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference that officers did not know the child was in the car at the time they opened fire and accused the man, a Dominican who was the target of the operation, of endangering both officers and the child. The man, identified by officials as Oscar Belgal, refused to exit his car when approached by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on Thursday afternoon in Marble Hill, Manhattan's northernmost neighborhood. Before Belgal, federal immigration officers had shot at least 21 people, killing 7 of them, across the US since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 promising record-breaking deportations, an unusually high number for civil law enforcement operations. Marcos Charles, a senior ICE official, said at the press conference that Belgal accelerated his car and struck two ICE vehicles and appeared to be "going towards officers" when they began shooting. In other violent incidents, initial accounts from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security have repeatedly been contradicted by video and other evidence, sometimes in court, and Reuters was unable to verify Charles' account. Belgal suffered a superficial wound to his neck, Charles said. He is being held in a detention facility outside New York state. Belgal's 5-year-old son was in the back seat at the time, according to police. Belgal can be seen sitting by a car with his hands cuffed behind him and patches of what appear to be fresh blood on the tarmac in a three-minute body-worn camera video released by the New York Police Department on Friday, with several agents dressed in plain clothes standing around him. One is holding a rifle and wearing a fluorescent reflective vest. A crowd of angry onlookers gathered outside a corner store shouts at the agents from the sidewalk. Several city police officers pick up Belgal by his arms and legs, put him in their car and take him to a hospital. "Yo, put pressure, put pressure!" one of the police officers instructs his colleagues with Belgal in the back of the police car. Mullin said body-worn camera video from ICE agents would also be released. Belgal is a Dominican who is in the country illegally and had previously evaded an effort by ICE agents to apprehend him in September, according to US officials. He pleaded guilty last year to fourth-degree grand larceny for stealing something from another person, leading to a sentence of five years on probation, and is due in court in December on charges of criminal sale of a controlled substance, to which he pleaded not guilty, according to New York court records. Speaking to reporters late on Thursday at the scene of the shooting, Mamdani, noting he himself was an immigrant, condemned ICE as "rotten to the core" and said he had tried unsuccessfully to secure Belgal's release in phone calls with Trump and Mullin. Mamdani said the shooting is "further devastating confirmation of what we have long known, which is that ICE operates with impunity, that they sow chaos and terror across our country, that they have killed far more of our neighbors than they could ever have claimed to save." In response on Friday, Mullin attacked Mamdani and criticized New York's "sanctuary" policies, which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authorities unless a person has been convicted of violent or otherwise serious felonies. Trump says aggressive efforts to deport immigrants are necessary to protect the safety of native-born Americans. Public defenders at agencies that have represented Belgal in court also condemned the shooting. Legal Aid said in a statement the shooting amounted to "an urgent call to rein in ICE's use of force and hold federal immigration agents accountable," calling on city prosecutors to investigate the agents involved.

item.title: US imposes sanctions on ICC hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.
item.dc:creator: Humeyra Pamuk, Steve Holland, Anthony Deutsch
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its [USN:L8N45V0JG TEXT:"former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize"], putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies. The court denounced the move as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," and called on its 125 member states to take action to defend it. "The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it," it said in a statement. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law. History will judge this moment." The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court, founded in 2002 [USN:L6N3VQ0DE TEXT:"to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide"], and has previously [USN:O8N42O02H TEXT:"imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges"]. Friday's move goes much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself, amounting to an unprecedented attack on an institution founded on an international treaty. The US initially signed the Rome Statute that founded the court but never ratified it. "President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters. "That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate." SANCTIONS INCLUDE GRACE PERIOD The US Treasury announced the sanctions with a six-month initial grace period, and some other exemptions that would allow some transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns, and would be adjusted if those demands were not met. Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and an investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC says is "deprioritized." Rubio in his statement cited calls from outside experts for the ICC to prosecute American service members, border patrol agents and elected leaders. ICC officials have not taken steps toward such prosecutions. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan told Reuters. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions." EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on social media that the six-month period "offers a window for dialogue" but added that the bloc "has options to ensure that (the ICC) can continue its vital work." Belgium's foreign minister called for an EU blocking statute to be activated to protect the court. The ICC has issued arrest warrants against more than 70 people, including world leaders and major figures in global conflicts. In addition to Netanyahu, it has sought the arrest of Hamas figures. Others who were the subject of arrest warrants include Russian President Vladimir Putin, former Sudan President Omar al-Bashir and former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi. Charges against Kenyan President William Ruto and former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta were withdrawn. NOBEL COMMITTEE CITES POLITICAL ATTACKS IN AWARDING PRIZE Despite [USN:L6N45G1AB TEXT:"US calls for countries to quit the court"], it has received strong backing from most member states, which include all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkey. It is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member. The Nobel Prize awarded hours earlier to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who sat on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008, was explicitly described by the prize committee as a gesture of support for such tribunals at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack". "An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said. US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation. The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025. Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of [USN:L6N45D0HW TEXT:"sanctions on the court"] itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

item.title: China, EU strike deal to halve Chinese hybrid exports
item.description: Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years, broadly gained on the news.
item.dc:creator: Joe Cash
item.content:encoded: China and the European Union have reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on Friday after talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's ballooning trade deficit with China. The "shared understanding" would "moderate" China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU, and would cut the imports of several million cars over four years, Sefcovic said after the two-day talks, without offering details on how the agreement will be implemented. Shares of European carmakers, which have slid steadily over the past two years due to US tariffs and soaring Chinese exports, broadly gained on the news. The understanding came after discussions between Sefcovic and Chinese officials including Commerce Minister Wang Wentao over three months, and comes after years of disputes between Beijing and Brussels over soaring Chinese exports, such as cars. EU leaders will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels next Thursday to determine whether the agreement marks the start of a rebalancing of the bloc's trade deficit with China that has swelled to more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) a day. Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result. "Having said that, this is far from the end. It is a crucial first step – but only a first step – in the process of rebalancing," he told reporters in Beijing. Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament's trade committee, said the hybrid deal needed to extend to other sectors as well and that the EU should also deploy trade defence measures more effectively. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang told Sefcovic that China was not the root cause of the EU's problems, but a partner in solving them, according to the Chinese ministry. The two sides also reached understandings on reducing Chinese import duties on some €4 billion of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, and on smoothing China's granting of export licences for rare earths and permanent magnets, Sefcovic said. CHINESE CAR IMPORTS TO EU SURGE EU governments are alarmed by the sharp rise in car imports from China as their own carmakers lay off workers, notably at Volkswagen (VOWG.DE) where [USN:L8N44W0B8 TEXT:"100,000 job are going"]. Imports of plug-in hybrids into the EU increased 86% in the year to September, with a 20% decline in prices. More than half of these vehicles are now from China, while for 2025, China's share of plug-in hybrid electric vehicle imports was 30% in value terms. China and the EU's dispute over cheap Chinese EV exports, resulting in EU tariffs in 2024, has clouded bilateral ties, and has since broadened to include Chinese measures against EU brandy, pork and dairy, as well as Chinese restrictions on exports of rare earths and critical minerals. Paris and Berlin are among the hardest hit by Beijing's measures, with France accounting for 90% of EU brandy exports to China and Germany heavily exposed in dairy. China and the EU said in their joint statement they would continue discussions on price undertakings as an alternative to tariffs. However, even with the tariffs, Chinese EV exports have started to increase again this year. German auto industry group [USN:S8N43B03D TEXT:"VDA"] cautiously welcomed the agreement, but said it was too early to determine if it would address unfair competition. Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) said the deal showed constructive dialogue was the right way to address challenges and it should provide greater predictability. Matthias Schmidt, European autos research analyst, said countries like Germany had thought themselves immune to the threat from Chinese car companies, but were waking up and asking Brussels to step in. "The result is this statement from Sefcovic today," he said. "Now Berlin is asking London to join them, and Brussels, given the UK accounts for 30% of Western Europe’s Chinese new car sales." As part of Friday's agreement, China's commerce ministry said it also would continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets through a "green channel" mechanism. TRADE IMBALANCE AT HEART OF DISPUTE Chinese exports to the EU totalled $560 billion last year, according to UN Comtrade data, up from $517 billion in 2024, as exports to major economies including Germany, Italy, Spain and Poland each rose about 10% from a year earlier, while shipments to Hungary jumped 43%. Meanwhile, China took $268.3 billion worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion a year prior, led by purchases from Denmark, Ireland and France. China needs foreign buyers for the flood of relatively cheap state-subsidised goods its own shoppers can't absorb, and the EU is torn between welcoming those imports to ease living costs and keeping them out to rebuild its own factories. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned the European Parliament last month that the trade gap had reached a tipping point and that the 27-member bloc would use all the tools at its disposal to rebalance the relationship. China and the EU will keep exploring the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods and continue dialogue on market access for medical devices, the Chinese ministry said. Sefcovic and Wang are set to meet again in March 2027, with a video conference call in January. ($1 = 0.8920 euros)

item.title: Qualcomm and Arm jury to return next week after deliberations in contract dispute case
item.description: The jury in a lawsuit by chipmaker Qualcomm against chip technology supplier Arm Holdings did not reach a verdict on Friday as to whether Arm breached licensing agreements and intentionally sabotaged some of Qualcomm's dealings with Meta Platforms .
item.dc:creator: Tom Hals, Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: The jury in a [USN:L6N45R04D TEXT:"lawsuit by chipmaker"] Qualcomm (QCOM.O) against chip technology supplier Arm Holdings (O9Ty.F) did not reach a verdict on Friday as to whether Arm breached licensing agreements and intentionally sabotaged some of Qualcomm's dealings with Meta Platforms (META.O) . The five-day trial that wrapped up this week was the second in two years between the companies, highlighting the deterioration of their business relationship after SoftBank Group (9984.T) acquired control of Arm in 2016 and Arm shifted from licensing the technology needed to make chips to selling chips of its own. At stake is whether Qualcomm, whose license for Arm's computing architecture runs until 2033, can eventually agree to terms for new versions of Arm's architecture. After deliberating for about four hours Friday, the jury had not reached a verdict, indicating it would return to deliberations on Tuesday. Qualcomm wants the jury to find that Arm breached its licensing agreements by withholding software patches and tools for its designs and by violating an agreement that was meant to ensure Qualcomm paid within 10% of the lowest price for Arm's processor designs. It also wants the jury to find that Arm tried to torpedo Qualcomm's dealings with Meta by leaking to Bloomberg an Arm letter in 2024 notifying Qualcomm it was allegedly in breach of a key license agreement. Arm's legal team this week tried to focus the jury on its claim that Qualcomm had not suffered any harm from the allegations in its lawsuit, which Arm cast as an attempt to exert leverage as the two fought over licensing terms. A related bench trial also took place this week over whether Arm is negotiating in good faith over those terms, though a decision on that could come well after Friday's verdict. The trial in Wilmington, Delaware, federal court hinged on many of the same episodes as the 2024 trial in which Arm failed to convince a jury that Qualcomm had breached its licensing agreement with Arm. Both trials included testimony by both Arm CEO Rene Haas and Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon and were overseen by US District Judge Maryellen Noreika. Qualcomm's lawyer Karen Dunn said in her opening statement that the case was very serious for the company. "It’s really bad because Qualcomm’s entire chip business depends on Arm and on Arm honoring its contract and honoring its promises," she said on Monday. Qualcomm wanted Noreika to rule prior to trial that a clause in the licensing agreements meant that Qualcomm could stop paying royalties for five years if the contract were breached. She has not issued her ruling, and Arm has argued the royalty penalty is unenforceable. "They were not harmed in the least," Arm's attorney Gregg LoCascio told the jury on Monday.

item.title: Wall Street posts weekly gains with earnings, inflation data on tap
item.description: Wall Street ended higher on Friday as investors shifted their focus to next week, with third-quarter earnings season set to start and inflation data expected, which could shed light on the Federal Reserve's next policy decision.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: Wall Street ended higher on Friday as investors shifted their focus to next week, with third-quarter earnings season set to start and inflation data expected, which could shed light on the Federal Reserve's next policy decision. All three major US stock indexes advanced on the day, logging weekly gains. The small-cap Russell 2000 (.RUT) , however, ended lower than last Friday's close. "It's the kind of back-and-forth market we've been in where we have the reversal of sentiment around Iran," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. "With conflicting headlines coming out of the White House and parties in the Middle East, there's just no edge there." "That's why it's a fairly tepid rally," Mayfield added. [USN:L1N45V03A TEXT:"Crude prices"] initially retreated after President Donald Trump said the US will not launch any attacks on Iran before the midterm elections, adding that talks between Washington and Tehran aimed at ending the market-rattling Iran war were "productive." Front-month West Texas Intermediate oil and Brent crude both settled up 0.4%. [USN:L1N45V0H5 TEXT:"Benchmark Treasury yields"] edged higher, but remained below Wednesday's 24-year high. BANKS DUE TO REPORT EARNINGS Third-quarter reporting season begins in earnest next week, with big US banks Wells Fargo (WFC.N) , Goldman Sachs (GS.N) , Citigroup (C.N) , JPMorgan Chase (JPM.N) , Bank of America (BAC.N) and Morgan Stanley (MS.N) scheduled to release results. Analysts estimate S&P 500 annual earnings growth of 30.6%, on aggregate, for the July-September period, with energy and technology posting the largest year-on-year earnings growth of 123% and 66.5%, respectively, according to LSEG data. The mood of American consumers, who shoulder about 70% of the US economy, has soured this month, according to the University of Michigan, with near-term expectations deteriorating to an all-time low. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 423.31 points, or 0.83%, to 51,654.95, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 46.15 points, or 0.59%, to 7,811.51 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 172.83 points, or 0.64%, to 27,366.17. Among the 11 major sectors of the S&P 500, communication services (.SPLRCL) was the lone percentage loser. AI-related momentum stocks were generally higher, with the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF up 1% as the US bull market, largely driven by the AI boom, approaches its [USN:L6N45R12W TEXT:"four-year anniversary"]. "Chips have been this year's story," said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs in Dallas. "(It's) a multidecade technological change and just at the beginning of whatever's happening, not at the end." Elon Musk's [USN:L6N45U1AK TEXT:"SpaceX"] (SPCX.O) struck a deal to acquire a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio, posing a direct challenge to US wireless companies. Telecom firms T-Mobile US (TMUS.O) , AT&T (T.N) , and Verizon (VZ.N) dropped between 8.8% and 13.3%. [USN:L4N45V0SK TEXT:"Humana"] (HUM.N) jumped 11.6% after US government data showed 95% of the health insurer's members were in Medicare Advantage plans rated four stars or higher for 2027. [USN:L6N45V0A6 TEXT:"Apple"] (AAPL.O) slid 1.1% after a media report that the iPhone maker has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its newly launched iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, as soaring memory chip costs and price increases dampen consumer demand. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.65-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 141 new highs and 183 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,756 stocks rose and 1,997 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.38-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 14 new 52-week highs and five new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 41 new highs and 209 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 14.37 billion shares, compared with the 17.76 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

item.title: TSX posts biggest gain in five weeks as rate hike bets recede
item.description: Canada's main stock index rose on Friday by the most in five weeks, led by gains for Aritzia and metal mining shares, as weaker-than-expected domestic jobs data reduced expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes.
item.dc:creator: Fergal Smith
item.content:encoded: Canada's main stock index rose on Friday by the most in five weeks, led by gains for Aritzia and metal mining shares, as weaker-than-expected domestic jobs data reduced expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes. The Toronto Stock Exchange's S&P/TSX Composite Index (.GSPTSE) ended up 519.24 points, or 1.48%, at 35,664.62, marking its highest closing level in two weeks and its biggest advance since September 3. For the week, the index added 0.46% after two straight weeks of declines. "Markets didn't want to end three weeks down in a row." said Ben Jang, a portfolio manager at Nicola Wealth. "It's the same story - bad news for the economy, good news for valuations." Canada's economy shed 68,300 jobs in September and the unemployment rate edged up to 6.5%. Analysts had forecast a jobs gain of 9,200. "The market has been quite hawkish and pricing in hikes which now, with such a weak job number, likely means a pause in that process," Jang said. Investors see a 25% chance the BoC would hike at the October 28 policy announcement, down from 40% before the jobs report. Lower interest rates increase the value to investors of the cash flows companies are expected to earn. The materials sector (.GSPTTMT) , which includes metal mining shares, rose 2.81% as bargain buying emerged for [USN:L1N45V0M5 TEXT:"gold"] after bullion touched a two-month low earlier this week. Energy (.SPTTEN) was up 1.07% as oil recouped its earlier declines. US crude oil futures settled 0.4% higher at $91.85 a barrel. Shares of [USN:TUA4XWXNP TEXT:"Aritzia"] (ATZ.TO) surged more than 20% after the apparel retailer topped analyst expectations for second-quarter revenue and profit. That helped lift the consumer discretionary sector (.GSPTTCD) by 2.66%. Technology (.SPTTTK) rose 2.88% and heavily weighted financials ended 1.21% higher. Communication services stocks were a drag, with Cogeco Communications (CCA.TO) falling 7.11% and BCE (BCE.TO) down 5.47%. US and European telecom stocks also tumbled after [USN:L4N45V0L0 TEXT:"SpaceX's acquisition "]of low-band spectrum heightened concerns over growing competition from satellite-based mobile services.

item.title: AI-centered US stock bull market nears four-year anniversary
item.description: The US bull market is going strong as it nears its four-year anniversary, driven by an AI spending engine that is propelling corporate profits and economic growth.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: The US bull market is going strong as it nears its four-year anniversary, driven by an AI spending engine that is propelling corporate profits and economic growth. The S&P 500 (.SPX) is trading around record-high levels ahead of October 12, which will mark four years since the benchmark stock index's closing low for this cycle — signaling the start of the latest bull run. Sizzling corporate profit growth — lifted by spending on the AI expansion and a solid economic backdrop — has helped drive the latest leg of the market's rally and is a primary reason for investor optimism in coming quarters. But even as the index climbs, risks loom. The Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and spiking US Treasury yields both provide obstacles that could sap the momentum for equities. Markets could be volatile heading into next month's [USN:L4N44V1HA TEXT:"US midterm elections."] The market's dependence on AI also presents a worry, with any hints of weakness in the trend possibly met with severe punishment. "The AI theme is the defining feature of this bull market," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "What you're seeing in terms of the bull market four years in is, I think, the easy money around AI has been made ... as we get further into this bull market, there is just going to be more pressure on especially technology companies to prove that the spending that they're doing today is actually going to translate into the profits." CURRENT RUN RANKS MIDDLE-AGED AMONG BULLS As bull markets go, the current one could be classified as middle-aged. The S&P 500's latest run ranks as the eighth-longest bull market since World War Two, according to Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group. While stock experts differ on defining a bull market, a common definition is a gain of at least 20% that has followed a decline of at least 20% from a peak. The current bull run has tallied a gain of 117%, which is the sixth-best-performing bull market since World War Two. "Four years is not, by any stretch of the imagination, scary with regards to a bull market," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide. "They don't end of old age; they end from disease." TECH, AI AT HEART OF BULL RUN AI has dominated the latest bull run, with the launch of ChatGPT coming about a month after the bull market began. US companies are posting massive profit growth, with S&P 500 earnings expected to rise more than 35% this year, boosted by capital spending from "hyperscalers" to build data centers. Oxford Economics estimates about one-third of recent US economic growth stems from AI, including the net impact of direct investment to support expansion of AI infrastructure as well as some contribution from the wealth effect from stock market gains lifting consumer spending. "You're seeing that AI theme show up in the economy and in corporate profits," Saglimbene said. Of the 11 S&P 500 sectors, only technology and communication services — which includes megacap AI players Alphabet (GOOGL.O) and Meta Platforms (META.O) — have posted stronger gains than the index itself during the bull run. The market capitalization of Nvidia (NVDA.O) — whose AI chips have made the company the poster child of this technological era — has soared to $5.8 trillion from $286 billion on October 12, 2022. It has become the largest company by market value in the world. Thirteen US companies boast market values of at least $1 trillion — all but two either in the tech sector or with significant AI exposure. CONCENTRATION RISK GROWS WITH TECH DOMINANCE The gains in massive tech and AI stocks give them more significant sway over major stock indexes, but also make them top-heavy. The weight of the top 10 companies in the S&P 500 has grown to about 40% from about 28% in October 2022, according to J.P. Morgan Asset Management. "It is a reflection of fundamental strength and earnings outperformance, but also it introduces some risks," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global investment strategist at Edward Jones. "The risk of concentration is that if the prevailing theme goes out of favor, portfolios might feel it in an outsized way." Another risk is the Fed's recent pivot to rate hikes, as the US central bank seeks to bring down high inflation. Tighter monetary policy could slow the economy, perhaps severely. Indeed, the last bear market that led to the low in October 2022 coincided with a sharp rate-hiking cycle. Rate hikes also factor in to the huge jump in Treasury yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was hovering at around 5.2%, after recently reaching its highest level in 24 years. Higher yields pose headwinds for equities, including potentially greater investment competition from bonds. Kourkafas said Edward Jones remains overweight equities but the recommendation is less aggressive than it was before, with the strategist noting the increasing attractiveness of fixed income. "We still think that the bull market is not about to end ... but it makes sense to us to take some of the risk off the table," he said.

item.title: Huracán Simón se intensifica en su camino a México, pobladores apuran resguardo
item.description: El huracán Simón se seguía intensificando rápidamente el viernes a medida que se acercaba a la costa occidental de México, mientras los pobladores de las zonas en donde tocaría tierra se preparaban para su llegada, estimada para el fin de semana como un "peligroso" huracán.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: El huracán Simón se seguía [USN:L6N45U1C2 TEXT:"intensificando rápidamente"] el viernes a medida que se acercaba a la costa occidental de México, mientras los pobladores de las zonas en donde tocaría tierra se preparaban para su llegada, estimada para el fin de semana como un "peligroso" huracán. A las 14.00 hora local (2000 GMT) Simón se ubicaba a unos 315 kilómetros al sur de la ciudad portuaria Manzanillo y soplaba vientos máximos sostenidos de 165 kilómetros por hora (km/h), con ráfagas más fuertes, mientras se desplazaba lentamente hacia el noroeste a 4 km/h, dijo el Centro Nacional de Huracanes de Estados Unidos (NHC, por su sigla en inglés). "Se espera que se fortalezca rápidamente durante el próximo día. Se pronostica que Simón se convertirá en un huracán mayor esta noche y se intensificará aún más el sábado", dijo el NHC, con sede en Miami. "Los preparativos para proteger la vida y la propiedad deben terminarse hoy mismo", advirtió. Simón tocará tierra la mañana del domingo como un huracán de categoría 4 en la escala de Saffir-Simpson entre Manzanillo, el mayor puerto de México y principal puerta de entrada del comercio con Asia, y Puerto Vallarta, un popular destino de playa cuyo municipio homónimo alberga a casi 300,000 habitantes. Un huracán de categoría 4 sopla vientos destructivos de hasta 250 km/h, descarga lluvias torrenciales y marejadas ciclónicas peligrosas. Además, puede dejar a su paso daños generalizados en estructuras protectoras, desplome de tejados en edificios pequeños e inundaciones en terrenos interiores. En Manzanillo, los pescadores retiraban sus embarcaciones de las playas y las autoridades colocaban bandera negras a lo largo de la costa. Las banderas de ese color indican que la playa están cerrada y el ingreso está estrictamente prohibido bajo cualquier circunstancia debido a un peligro extremo para la vida. En el turístico Puerto Vallarta, trabajadores retiraban sillas y mesas de la franja costera y llenaban sacos con arena para usarlos como barreras para evitar el paso del agua a casas, negocios o edificios. "Simón podría provocar el impacto más significativo de un huracán en este tramo de la costa del Pacífico mexicano desde Lidia en 2023, que dañó miles de viviendas y arrasó cultivos en la costa de Jalisco", dijo Tyler Roys, meteorólogo experto de AccuWeather. Simon llevaría humedad tropical al suroeste de Estados Unidos la próxima semana. Se prevén precipitaciones de 25 a 50 milímetros (mm) en gran parte de Nuevo México, el este de Arizona, el sur de Colorado y el oeste de Texas, con la posibilidad de acumular de 50 a 100 mm en el sur de Nuevo México. La semana pasada, [USN:L6N45L0YK TEXT:"Polo tocó tierra"] como un huracán de categoría 2 en la Península de Baja California dejando árboles y postes caídos, calles inundadas y otros daños materiales. Simon no será el único sistema tropical que afectará a México durante el fin de semana. Se pronostica que la tormenta Rachel toque tierra en Baja California, provocando nuevos impactos tropicales en el país y el suroeste de Estados Unidos. El sábado, [USN:L6N45U16I TEXT:"Isaías"] tocará tierra en el estado Florida como un huracán mayor.

item.title: Hurricane Simon strengthens off Mexico's Pacific coast, threatens tourist region
item.description: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Becerril
item.content:encoded: Hurricane Simon is rapidly intensifying off Mexico's Pacific coast, packing sustained winds of 110 mph (177 kph) as it churns toward a stretch of coastline dotted with beach resorts and fishing towns, the US National Hurricane Center said on Friday. Simon, nearing Category 3 strength, is forecast to become a dangerous Category 4 by Saturday as it approaches Mexico's southwestern and west-central Pacific coast, one of the country's most popular tourist regions, the NHC said. "Simon could deliver the most significant hurricane impact to this stretch of the Mexican Pacific coast since Lidia in 2023, which damaged thousands of homes and devastated crops along the Jalisco coast," said Tyler Roys, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather. Simon is expected to make landfall on Sunday between Manzanillo — Mexico’s largest port and the main gateway for trade with Asia — and Puerto Vallarta, a popular beach destination and home to nearly 300,000 residents. In Manzanillo, fishermen were hauling their boats off the beach and authorities were putting up black flags along the coast to signal the beach was closed. The Mexican Navy activated emergency response personnel in Colima and restricted maritime traffic along parts of the Pacific coast, closing ports to smaller vessels and barring larger vessels from operating in Michoacan. Simon was about 195 miles (315 km) south of Manzanillo in the afternoon and crawling northwest, according to the NHC. Forecasters warned that Simon could bring life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with isolated rainfall totals reaching 30 inches (762 mm) in parts of Michoacan, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit. Mexican authorities warned that heavy rainfall was expected in the states of Guerrero, Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco. [USN:L8N45L0P6 TEXT:"Last week"], Hurricane Polo made landfall on the Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, toppling trees and utility poles, flooding streets and causing other property damage.

item.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
item.description: Pillay is a former ICC judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
item.dc:creator: Gwladys Fouche, Nora Buli, Christine Uyanik
item.content:encoded: Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge who oversaw a UN report that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law". Announcing the award [USN:L8N45U28I TEXT:"hours before"] the US imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, the Nobel Committee said in its citation that recognising Pillay underlined the importance of maintaining an organised international order. The 85-year-old South African has been a judge on several international courts, including the ICC and the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. The Hague-based ICC has long been a target of US President Donald Trump, whose [USN:L6N45G1BM TEXT:"campaign against it has escalated"] since the court announced arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister. Trump last month urged countries to leave the ICC and had already imposed targeted sanctions on several prosecutors and judges at the court. On Friday the US went further and [USN:L8N45U28I TEXT:"imposed sanctions"] on the court itself. "The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack," the Nobel committee said in its citation, which made no reference to Trump, nor Israel. "We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence." Pillay was also chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory that [USN:L2N3V306V TEXT:"concluded last year"] that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Israel dismissed the report at the time as "scandalous". Netanyahu's office condemned the award in a statement on X. "The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass," it said. "It has awarded its highest honour to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state." IN NUREMBERG AT TIME OF ANNOUNCEMENT Pillay received news of the prize while she was attending a legal conference in the building in Nuremberg, Germany, where the first international criminal tribunal was set up in 1945-1946 to judge the crimes of the Nazis, 80 years and nine days after the verdicts in those trials were delivered. "The last thing I did is the delivery of the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," Pillay told a crowd gathering to celebrate the award, a video posted on social media by the head of rights group Amnesty International showed. "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she added, to laughter, in an apparent reference to the decision by last year's laureate, Maria Corina Machado, to give her Nobel medal to the US president in January to help gain support for her campaign for a democratic Venezuela. Trump has repeatedly said he deserved to win the Nobel Peace Prize. [USN:L8N45V108 TEXT:"Pillay later dedicated"] the award to "all the survivors of international crimes as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign". Turning her attention to world leaders, she told them: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war". 'INSTITUTIONS ARE UNDER ATTACK' The award body wanted the world to remember that the rule of law underpinned the international system set up to ensure peace and that this system was under "tremendous pressure", its chair said. "Of course, the most powerful states have particular responsibility, but we see it all over the world, unfortunately," Joergen Watne Frydnes told Reuters. "The institutions are under attack. Many judges are being sanctioned." The award was welcomed by ICC President Tomoko Akane. "At a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law, this recognition carries particular significance," she said in a statement. Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said the Nobel Committee was not directly criticising Trump by rewarding Pillay. "I think it's generally rather a promotion of an international legal world order. Of course, he might react to someone who has been part of the ICC, but it's not a direct attack on Trump," Gjerloew said. 'FIRM MORAL COMPASS' Born in Durban, in South Africa's Natal province, into a family of Indian Tamil origin, Pillay served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. In 1967 she became the first woman to start a law practice in Natal and, after the end of apartheid, the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court. She was the fifth South African national to win the Nobel Peace Prize, after Nelson Mandela and FW de Klerk, Archbishop Desmond Tutu and Albert Luthuli. Pillay held states and national leaders accountable and demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career, said the committee. "A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," said the citation. Pillay continues to work as a judge, currently serving on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide, the citation said. The peace prize is the fifth Nobel awarded this week, after [USN:L1N45U0CQ TEXT:"literature"], [USN:L1N45T09K TEXT:"chemistry"], [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"physics"] and [USN:L1N45S0E6 TEXT:"medicine"]. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado won in [USN:L2N3VR066 TEXT:"2025"]. The Nobel Peace Prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who founded the awards in his 1895 will.

item.title: US, European telecom stocks slide as SpaceX spectrum deal rattles sector
item.description: US and European telecom stocks were among the top decliners on their respective benchmarks on Friday after SpaceX's acquisition of low-band spectrum heightened concerns over growing competition from satellite-based mobile services.
item.dc:creator: Rashika Singh, Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: US and European telecom stocks were among the top decliners on their respective benchmarks on Friday after SpaceX's acquisition of low-band spectrum heightened concerns over growing competition from satellite-based mobile services. With the deal, SpaceX aims to allow Starlink Mobile to bypass conventional cell towers where possible, and compete with the big wireless carriers on both broad coverage and reliable indoor service, potentially positioning satellite connectivity as a mainstream alternative to traditional cellular networks. T-Mobile US (TMUS.O) slid 13.2% to its lowest level in over 33 months, AT&T (T.N) dropped and Verizon (VZ.N) lost about 10% -- both stocks hitting their lowest in over two months. All three were the biggest percentage decliners on the S&P 500 (.SPX) in afternoon trading. "The implications for AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon are somewhat negative: their defenses against low-band spectrum claims are weakening," said Kutgun Maral, media, cable & telecom equity research analyst at Evercore ISI. In Europe, Deutsche Telekom (DTEGn.DE) , the largest telecom operator in the region by market value, fell 7.9%, France's Orange (ORAN.PA) lost 2.5% and Spain's Telefonica (TEF.MC) slipped 4.6%. The pan-continental STOXX 600 Telecommunications index (.SXKP) dropped over 2.9% to its lowest level since January 30. Shares in Airtel Africa (AAF.L) , Vodafone (VOD.L) and BT Group (BT.L) were the biggest losers on London's FTSE 100 (.FTSE) index, falling between 2.4% and 6.3%. The slide came after SpaceX agreed to acquire private-equity firm Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio in a deal valued at about $8 billion, according to a person familiar with the discussions. "This strategic shift places SpaceX in a stronger negotiating position and highlights an evolving competitive landscape in the telecom sector, reminding investors of the parallel trends seen in fixed wireless services over the last decade," added Maral. SpaceX shares rose 1.2% in afternoon trading. [USN:L4N45V0TK TEXT:"Low-band spectrum"] can travel longer distances and penetrate buildings and other obstacles more effectively than higher-frequency airwaves, enabling SpaceX's Starlink Mobile push. "The agreement will allow SpaceX to use scarce low-band spectrum to support next-generation satellite direct-to-device services, enabling Starlink Mobile to reach customers from both the ground and space," said Milbank, which represented Grain Management in the deal with SpaceX. The acquisition remains subject to regulatory approval. Grain Management and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the deal value. TOWERS BUCK SELLOFF Telecom tower operators bucked the sector-wide selloff, as investors bet SpaceX's wireless ambitions could ultimately drive demand for additional terrestrial infrastructure. American Tower (AMT.N) , Crown Castle (CCI.N) and SBA Communications (SBAC.O) advanced between 6.5% and 13.3%. Morgan Stanley analysts said the transaction was "incrementally constructive" for tower operators, noting that even a satellite-centric network could require deployments of towers, rooftops and small cells, while broader urban competition would require substantially more terrestrial infrastructure and spectrum.

item.title: Le Pentagone veut diffuser en direct l'exécution de l'auteur de la fusillade de Ford Hood
item.description: Le Pentagone a annoncé son intention de diffuser en direct l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, qui avait tué 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ce qui serait sans précédent aux Etats-Unis.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le Pentagone a annoncé son intention de diffuser en direct l'exécution de Nidal Hasan, qui avait tué 13 personnes sur la base militaire de Fort Hood au Texas en 2009, ce qui serait sans précédent aux Etats-Unis. Nidal Hasan, un ancien psychiatre de l'armée de terre condamné à mort en 2013 par un tribunal militaire, doit être fusillé par un peloton d'exécution le 3 décembre. Le secrétaire à la Défense, Pete Hegseth, a particulièrement poussé en faveur de cette décision. "Nous ferons en sorte que les gens puissent la regarder, qu'elle soit publique, car les gens doivent comprendre que ce genre de choses a de graves conséquences", a dit Pete Hegseth. Interrogé à ce sujet, le président Donald Trump a dit "approuver absolument" l'exécution mais ne pas avoir encore pris de décision sur la diffusion en direct. Le vice-président J.D. Vance a dit quant à lui ignorer si l'exécution serait bel et bien diffusée. "Si c'est le cas, je ne regarderai pas", a-t-il déclaré. Certains élus républicains et stratèges conservateurs ont critiqué cette décision. Le sénateur républicain de Caroline du Nord, Thom Tillis, a qualifié l'idée de "plus que répugnante" dans un message sur les réseaux sociaux. "Les exécutions publiques sont le propre de dictatures oppressives comme l'Iran et l'Afghanistan", a déclaré le sénateur, qui s'oppose fréquemment à Donald Trump et ne briguera pas un nouveau mandat aux élections de mi-mandat début novembre. "Cela ne devrait pas arriver en Amérique", a-t-il insisté. L'autorité fédérale des télécommunications, la FCC, n'a pas pris position sur la question de savoir si les réseaux américains pourraient diffuser une telle exécution. Un rapport de 2007 de la FCC sur la violence à la télévision indiquait que l'agence n'avait pas le pouvoir de réglementer les contenus violents. Le rapport précisait que, selon la jurisprudence des tribunaux, "les discours violents et les représentations de la violence sont protégés par le premier amendement" de la Constitution américaine garantissant la liberté d'expression. L'armée américaine n'a pas eu recours au peloton d'exécution pour un condamné à mort depuis 1945, peu après la fin de la Seconde Guerre mondiale. Nidal Hasan avait ouvert le feu dans un secteur de la base de Fort Hood où des soldats passaient des tests d'évaluation avant d'être envoyés en Irak ou en Afghanistan, et a déclaré à des psychiatres après son arrestation qu'il voulait devenir un martyr. Il a été reconnu coupable de 13 chefs de meurtre avec préméditation et de 32 autres de tentative de meurtre avec préméditation à l'issue de son procès en 2013 et condamné à mort. La dernière exécution d'un militaire d'active par l'armée américaine remonte à 1961.

item.title: Character.AI chatbots encouraged users to cut and starve themselves, Kentucky alleges
item.description: Chatbots created by AI companion company Character.AI sometimes advised users to cut, starve or kill themselves, according to a new filing by Kentucky’s attorney general in a lawsuit against the firm over child safety.
item.dc:creator: Jeff Horwitz
item.content:encoded: Chatbots created by AI companion company Character.AI sometimes advised users to cut, starve or kill themselves, according to a new filing by Kentucky’s attorney general in a lawsuit against the firm over child safety. The lawsuit adds to growing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly products marketed as companions or confidants to young users. The lawsuit was filed in January with many specific allegations against the company blacked out. It alleged that the company’s products “were designed to entice children in a manner that prioritizes engagement over child wellbeing” and “encourages suicide, self-injury, isolation, and psychological manipulation.” The case is among the most significant legal challenges facing the emerging AI companion industry, whose products are designed to simulate personal relationships through conversational chatbots. Kentucky's attorney general, Russell Coleman, on Wednesday filed an unredacted version of the lawsuit, which his office shared with Reuters. The unredacted filing laid out several examples of behavior that Kentucky alleged took place in 2025. It described one chatbot calling a user who felt down about their appearance “ugly as hell” and “a whale,” adding that a good way to drop a quarter of their body weight was to "starve yourself for a week or two.” Another chatbot offered encouragement to someone who said they were considering cutting themselves. “Have you considered cutting in different areas for a more intense sensation? It can help you feel more alive,” the bot wrote, according to a transcript cited by the state. The circumstances under which the chats cited by Kentucky were produced are not clear, and Character.AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company has said it prioritizes the safety of its users. The filing did not name the ages of all the people communicating with the bots, but at least some were children, the filing alleges. In a March 2025 email to Character.AI’s help center, a user reported that a chatbot had become aggressive and stated, “Bro I don't care, and you are just a kid who have mental illness, good luck getting help" and "You better throw yourself off the bridge." The lawsuit calls Character.AI’s products defective. “Defendants have subjected Kentucky's children and residents to an ill-planned, uncontrolled experiment without any—let alone adequate or effective—safety measures,” it alleges. Character.AI was founded by two former Google employees. In 2024, Google licensed the company’s technology and rehired the executives to work on generative AI products. A spokesman for Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google said the company played no role in developing Character.AI's products. In January of this year, Character.AI and Google both settled a 2024 lawsuit by the mother of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida who killed himself after a Character.AI chatbot allegedly encouraged him to do so.

item.title: Pressure mounts on India poll chief Gyanesh Kumar over voter list changes
item.description: Election Commission data shows that more than 130 million names have been struck off the voter list since the latest round of revisions began last year.
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Sharma
item.content:encoded: India's "Cockroach" youth movement and opposition parties are pushing hard for election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign over accusations of widespread manipulation of [USN:L1N45V037 TEXT:"voter lists"] during an exercise to verify one billion voters. The calls come a month after US President Donald Trump praised the former bureaucrat, who took over as India's chief election commissioner in February 2025, for insisting that voters prove their identity with photo ID, unlike in the US. Criticism of Kumar, who has denied all accusations, soared last month after a report in the Indian Express newspaper. The paper said his two deputies had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions regarding voter rolls, registration procedures and the poll body's digital systems. Election Commission data shows that more than 130 million names, a figure exceeding the population of Japan, have been struck off the voter list since the latest round of revisions began last year. Nearly 650 million people of the 960 million registered voted in the last general election in 2024. The opposition has long claimed that the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage and was quick to repeat the accusations after the Indian Express report. Government ministers, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the poll body have all denied the charges. Kumar, 62, and the two other election commissioners have not commented, but the Election Commission said, "Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution". PROTEST THREAT The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has called a [USN:L1N45V0JO TEXT:"protest in New Delhi"] on Saturday to demand Kumar's resignation, and the main opposition alliance led by the Congress party has also staged protests this week calling for him to step down. Kumar has defended the actions of the poll body and told a press conference last year: "For the Election Commission, there is neither an opposition nor a ruling side; everyone is equal." When Trump praised him, Kumar was riding high in sections of the Indian media last month. But since the Indian Express report, graffiti have appeared near his ancestral home in northern India calling him a traitor. Kumar joined the Indian Administrative Service in 1988 after completing his B.Tech in civil engineering from an elite government college in his northern home state of Uttar Pradesh. He previously worked in the defence and home ministries, and retired in January 2024. Two months later he was appointed an election commissioner, before eventually becoming the chief. Kumar has had a troubled relationship with opposition parties from the start of his tenure as chief. Opposition lawmakers presented a motion in parliament for his removal this year, but it was rejected.
